title: Legal Aid
lead: India's legal aid system gives statutory teeth to ==Article 39A== through the ==Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987==, in force from ==9 November 1995== — now ==National Legal Services Day==.

items: ==s.12==: eligibility criteria for free legal services.
==ss.19–22==: organisation of ==Lok Adalats==; awards are ==deemed decrees of a civil court — final, binding, non-appealable==.
==ss.22A–22E (2002 Amendment)==: ==Permanent Lok Adalats== for pre-litigation conciliation of ==public utility service== disputes (transport, postal, electricity, water, hospitals, insurance).
==1994 & 2002 Amendments==: broadened legal aid, introduced Permanent Lok Adalats, refined the institutional hierarchy.

==Allied instruments==: ==s.341 BNSS== (State pleader for an accused before a Court of Session); ==NALSA (Free and Competent Legal Services) Regulations, 2010==; State Model Rules; ==Tele-Law (2017)== and ==Nyaya Bandhu== pro bono programme.

items.title: Dispute Resolution Arms
bullets: ==Lok Adalats== — conciliatory settlement of pending and pre-litigation cases; awards have decree force with ==no appeal==; ==court fees refunded==
==Permanent Lok Adalats== — standing bodies with ==adjudicatory (not merely conciliatory)== powers for public utility disputes up to a pecuniary limit
==Mediation and Family Court linkages== — court-attached mediation centres to decongest dockets

==Tele-Law== — video/telephone advice via Common Service Centres
==Nyaya Bandhu== app connecting citizens with volunteering advocates
==Victim Compensation Schemes== via DLSAs; NGOs and Bar Associations (e.g. Human Rights Law Network)

items: ==Poor quality of representation== — legal aid lawyers overburdened, underpaid (fees far below market), sometimes inexperienced → legal aid seen as a ==symbolic rather than substantive right==.
==Low public awareness== — many eligible beneficiaries in rural and tribal areas don't know legal aid exists.
==Inadequate funding== — budget constraints limit empanelled lawyers, PLVs and outreach camps.
==Understaffing== — chronic DLSA secretary vacancies; shortage of panel lawyers in remote and LWE-affected districts.
==Coordination gaps== between DLSAs, police, prisons and judiciary delay identification of eligible undertrials.
==Quality vs quantity in Lok Adalats== — disposal pressure can produce settlements through ==pressure to compromise rather than genuine consent==.
==Digital divide== limits Tele-Law's reach; ==gender and social barriers== (stigma, mobility, patriarchal control) deter women and marginalised groups.
==Weak monitoring== — little outcome-based evaluation of whether legal aid improves case outcomes.
==Undertrial backlog== — many entitled to free legal aid and bail assistance don't access it in time.

items.title: Domestic
bullets: ==Nyaya Bandhu and Tele-Law== — legal aid integrated with digital platforms and Common Service Centres
==Legal Literacy Clubs in schools== — NALSA's scheme building a rights-conscious citizenry
==Village Legal Care and Support Centres== — run jointly with Panchayati Raj Institutions
==Prison Legal Aid Clinics== — assisting undertrials with bail applications and case status

items.title: Global
bullets: ==United States== — constitutionally mandated right to counsel ([[Gideon v. Wainwright, 1963]]) delivered through ==dedicated public defender offices==
==Netherlands== — a mixed model: public ==Legal Aid Board== plus subsidised private practitioners and ==‘law shops’== for early advice
==Finland== — ==universal public legal aid offices== with salaried lawyers and ==income-linked co-payment== rather than a strict eligibility cut-off

items: ==Quality assurance== — move toward a cadre of ==salaried, full-time legal aid defence counsel== (public defender model), at least in criminal matters
==Ring-fenced funding== — a fixed percentage of the judiciary/law ministry budget, plus better honoraria
==Expand PLV networks== — especially women and persons from marginalised communities as trusted intermediaries
==Deepen digital outreach while bridging the divide== — Tele-Law plus physical CSCs and offline camps
==Outcome-based monitoring== — an independent ==Justice Access Index== measuring outcomes, not case counts
==Proactive identification== — police and prisons must inform every eligible arrestee at the ==point of arrest==, with documented compliance
==Sensitisation and legal literacy== targeting women, SC/ST communities and persons with disabilities
==Safeguard voluntariness in Lok Adalats== — procedural safeguards against disposal-driven pressure
==Integrate with restorative justice== — link to victim compensation (==s.396 BNSS==) and rehabilitation support
